newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia has to persevere with fiscal stance - S&P.
newsitem.headline: Australia has to persevere with fiscal stance - S&P.

text.p: Standard & Poor's Corp said the Australian government will need to persevere with its tough fiscal stance over the next few of years before the rating agency will consider upgrading the country's rating.

"We see an upgrade as a possibility over the next couple of years really contingent on further evidence that the existing government will perservere with its fiscal tightening," the rating agency's New York-based chief sovereign analyst, David Beers told Reuters Financial Television.
Beers is currently in Sydney as part of the rating agency's annual review process of Australia.
S&P affirmed Australia's AA long-term and A1-plus short-term ratings on foreign currency debt, and its positive outlook, following the government's 1997/98 budget, announced in May.
Beers said he recognised that there is a relatively short electoral cycle here in Australia with election every three years and that the current government was elected last year.
"We want to see how they perform in the consistency of what they have promised on their fiscal policy and what they deliver," Beers said.

"The key thing here is for the government to persist in its deficit reduction because that in turn will reduce its external debt burden to levels that are more consistent with sovereigns rated in the AA plus category," Beers said.

In the May budget the Australian government projected an underlying budget deficit of A$3.9 billion for 1997/98 (July-June) moving to surpluses of A$1.6 billion in 1998/99, A$5.4 billion in 1999/2000 and A$10.4 billion the year after that.
S&P first put Australia on positive outlook following the Coaliation Liberal-National government's first budget in August 1996.
Beers said that while the rating agency affirmed Australia's ratings in May it would give a full review of the country in the coming weeks.
